title: American Literature, 1620–1920
bigQuestion: Three centuries of American writers disagreed about what America is; what did each of them say, and who answered whom?

story.title: One Night in the Concord Jail
story.kicker: In the summer of 1846 a man who lived in a cabin by a pond refused to pay a tax, spent a night in a cell, and turned the night into an essay that reached Gandhi and King.
paragraphs: In July 1846 Henry David Thoreau walked into Concord, Massachusetts, to pick up a mended shoe. He was living alone in a small cabin he had built beside Walden Pond, a mile or so from town, trying to find out how little a person needed in order to live well. On the street he met the town's tax collector, who reminded him that he had not paid his poll tax, a flat tax charged to each adult man, in several years. Thoreau said he would not pay it. The collector locked him up.

The refusal was not about money. The United States had just gone to war with Mexico, a war that Thoreau and many others in New England saw as a scheme to extend slavery into new territory. Massachusetts also returned escaped slaves to their owners under federal law. Thoreau did not believe he could pay into a government that did those things and still call himself an honest man. Paying, he thought, would make him a small partner in the wrong.

He spent one night in the jail. By his own account he found it oddly pleasant: he talked with his cellmate, listened to the sounds of the town through the window, and felt he was seeing Concord from the inside for the first time. In the morning someone, probably a relative, paid the tax without asking him, and the jailer let him go. He collected his shoe, joined a huckleberry party, and was back in the woods within the hour.

Two years later he gave a lecture about the night, and in 1849 it was printed under the title Resistance to Civil Government. Later editors called it Civil Disobedience, and the name stuck. In it Thoreau argues that a person's conscience outranks the law, that a majority can be wrong, and that when a government does injustice, the right place for a just person may be its prison. He wrote it as an argument, not a diary, and it turned one night in a small-town cell into a permanent American position.

That is what this chapter is about: American writers arguing with their country and with one another. A Puritan poet writing love poems in a colony that suspected poetry. A preacher trying to frighten a congregation into grace. A pamphlet writer telling soldiers that the times try men's souls. A formerly enslaved man explaining how he learned to read against the law. A poet in a white dress who published almost nothing. Each of them answers a question the last one asked, and the argument is still going.
story.think: Thoreau said paying the tax would make him a partner in the government's wrongs. Is there a difference between obeying a law and approving of it? Where would you draw the line?

lessons.title: Anne Bradstreet and Puritan Poetry
lessons.mainIdea: The first published American poet was a Puritan woman whose plain, personal poems reveal both her faith and her doubts.
reading: In 1630 an eighteen-year-old named Anne Bradstreet crossed the Atlantic with her husband and parents to the Massachusetts Bay Colony. She later wrote that her heart rose against the new world at first, and then she submitted to it. She raised eight children in a settlement where winters killed and books were few. She also wrote poetry, at night. In 1650 a collection of her poems was printed in London under the title The Tenth Muse. It was the first published book of poems by a writer living in what became the United States.

The *Puritans* who founded the colony believed that God had made a covenant with them. Scripture was the final authority, and every person's soul was in daily danger. They distrusted ornament, in churches and in writing. They prized the *plain style*: clear, direct language that served truth rather than showing off. Bradstreet's best poems are plain in that sense. When her house burned in 1666 she wrote about walking past the ruins. She remembers the trunk and the chest where treasures had stood, and then reminds herself that her true home is in heaven.

The poems are also honest about the pull between this world and the next. In her poem to her husband she says that if two people were ever one, they are. If a man was ever loved by a wife, he is. That is not the voice of a woman who found this world easy to give up. The tension between loving what is here and trusting what is promised runs through her work. It is the first version of a tension that American writers have never stopped exploring.

Read Bradstreet for two things. First, for the plain style at its best, which later writers from Thoreau to Hemingway would return to. Second, for the sound of a real person inside a rigid system, keeping faith and keeping her own voice at the same time. That is a very American situation, and she got there first.

words.d: English Protestants who founded Massachusetts Bay in 1630, seeking a purified church and a society under God's law
clear, direct writing that avoids ornament in order to serve truth
a solemn agreement; the Puritans believed God had made one with them
decoration added for show; the Puritans distrusted it

look.title: A Puritan Love Poem
look.text: If ever two were one, then surely we. / If ever man were loved by wife, then thee; / If ever wife was happy in a man, / Compare with me, ye women, if you can.
look.cite: Anne Bradstreet, To My Dear and Loving Husband, published 1678
look.prompt: The lines are plain and personal, yet Puritans were taught to love God above all. What tension does a poem like this create for its writer?

check.q: Why is The Tenth Muse historically important?
choices: It was the first novel written in America
It was the first published book of poems by a writer living in the American colonies
It was the first book printed in Boston
It was the first poem about Walden Pond
check.why: Printed in London in 1650, it was the first book of poems by a colonial American writer.

check.q: What does the plain style value?
choices: Rhyme above all
Long ornamental sentences
Clear, direct language that serves truth
Latin and Greek vocabulary
check.why: Puritans distrusted ornament and prized clear language, and Bradstreet's best poems show it.

check.q: What tension does the lesson find in Bradstreet's poems?
choices: Between loving this world and trusting the next
Between English and American spelling
Between rhyme and free verse
Between city and country life
check.why: Her love for husband and home pulls against the Puritan teaching that heaven is the true home.

lessons.title: Jonathan Edwards and the Sermon
lessons.mainIdea: Edwards's famous sermon uses vivid images and relentless logic to make an abstract doctrine feel like physical danger.
reading: On July 8, 1741, in Enfield, Connecticut, a minister named Jonathan Edwards read a sermon in a level voice. By several accounts, the congregation began to weep and cry out before he finished. Its title was Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God. Edwards was one of the most brilliant minds in the colonies, a philosopher as well as a preacher. He was part of the *Great Awakening*, a wave of intense religious revival that swept the colonies in the 1730s and 1740s.

The sermon's argument is simple: nothing but God's choice keeps any sinner out of hell at this moment, and God owes no one that choice. What makes the sermon literature is its *imagery*. Edwards compares the listener to a spider held over a fire by a thread, to a person walking on a rotten covering over a pit, to water dammed up and rising. Every image turns an idea about the soul into a body in danger. The listener does not think about damnation; the listener feels the thread.

Notice the method, because it is a method every persuasive writer can use. Edwards states a doctrine, then finds a physical picture for it, then repeats the picture with variations until the mind cannot escape it. He also speaks directly to the listener, in the second person, so that no one in the room can assume he means someone else. The sermon is an *argument* aimed at the body as much as the mind.

Edwards and Bradstreet share a faith and a colony but not a tone. She writes quietly of love and loss; he writes to terrify people toward grace. Reading them together you meet the two faces of Puritan writing: the private conscience and the public warning. American literature would keep both voices, and later writers would argue with each.

words.d: a wave of intense religious revival in the American colonies in the 1730s and 1740s
language that appeals to the senses, creating pictures the reader can see or feel
a speech on a religious subject given to a congregation
addressing the reader or listener directly as 'you'

look.title: The Spider Over the Fire
look.text: Edwards tells his listeners that God holds them over the pit of hell the way a person might hold a spider or some loathsome insect over a fire, that God is provoked by them, and that nothing but his hand keeps them from falling at this very moment.
look.cite: Jonathan Edwards, Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, 1741 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why a spider, and not a sinner, in the image? What does the choice of a small, disliked creature do to the listener's picture of themselves?

check.q: What does the lesson say makes Edwards's sermon literature rather than only doctrine?
choices: Its length
Its physical imagery, which makes an idea feel like bodily danger
Its use of Latin
Its calm ending
check.why: The spider, the rotten covering and the rising water turn an abstract teaching into a felt threat.

check.q: Why does Edwards use the second person?
choices: To sound humble
To quote the Bible more easily
So no listener can assume he means someone else
Because sermons were required to use it
check.why: Direct address makes each listener the subject of the warning.

check.q: How does the lesson contrast Bradstreet and Edwards?
choices: Private conscience versus public warning
Poetry versus fiction
Faith versus doubt
English versus American subjects
check.why: She writes quietly of love and loss; he writes to frighten a whole congregation toward grace.

lessons.title: Paine and the Pamphlet
lessons.mainIdea: Thomas Paine's pamphlets turned the argument for independence into plain, urgent prose that ordinary readers could repeat.
reading: In January 1776 a forty-seven-page pamphlet appeared in Philadelphia. It was called Common Sense, its author was unnamed, and within months it had sold more copies, for its population, than almost any publication in American history. The author was Thomas Paine, an Englishman who had arrived in the colonies barely a year earlier. His argument was that the colonies should not merely resist the king's taxes but separate from Britain entirely, and that the idea of kings was itself absurd.

A *pamphlet* is a short, cheap, unbound printed argument, and in the 1770s it was the fastest way to reach a public. Paine's genius was his style. Where lawyers and ministers wrote in long, learned sentences, Paine wrote as if talking across a table: short claims, homely comparisons, direct challenges. He called hereditary monarchy a joke played by nature, and asked why an island should govern a continent. Readers who had never read a political argument read his aloud in taverns.

In December 1776 Washington's army was shrinking and retreating across New Jersey. Paine published the first of a series he called The American Crisis. Its opening sentence, that these are the times that try men's souls, was reportedly read to the troops before they crossed the Delaware. The sentence works by *contrast*. The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot quit when it gets hard. Against them stands the one who stands it now and deserves the love and thanks of man and woman.

Paine shows how the Revolution was also a revolution in prose. The argument for independence was made not only in the Declaration's formal periods but in language a farmer or a private could carry in his head. Later American writers who trusted plain speech, from Lincoln to Twain, were working in a tradition Paine helped make. Notice, too, that Paine answers the Puritans: for them, the danger was the soul; for him, the danger was the king, and the remedy was in human hands.

words.d: a short, cheap, unbound printed argument meant for a wide public
rule by kings whose power passes to their children
setting two things side by side to sharpen the difference between them
full separation from British rule, Paine's goal in Common Sense

look.title: The Times That Try Men's Souls
look.text: These are the times that try men's souls: the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of his country; but he that stands it now, deserves the love and thanks of man and woman.
look.cite: Thomas Paine, The American Crisis, Number I, December 1776
look.prompt: Find the contrast in the sentence. Why might Paine name the quitters first and the one who stands second?

check.q: What did Common Sense argue?
choices: That the colonies should pay the king's taxes
That the colonies should separate from Britain entirely
That Massachusetts should leave the other colonies
That the war should be settled by treaty
check.why: Paine argued for full independence and mocked the idea of hereditary kings.

check.q: How did Paine's style differ from the lawyers and ministers of his day?
choices: He wrote only in verse
He used long Latin sentences
He refused to publish his work
He wrote as if talking across a table, with short claims and homely comparisons
check.why: His plain, direct prose let ordinary readers repeat the argument aloud.

check.q: In the opening of The American Crisis, which device makes the sentence work?
choices: Contrast between those who quit and the one who stands
A flashback to earlier battles
Stream of consciousness
Allusion to the Bible
check.why: The summer soldier and sunshine patriot are set against the one who stands it now.

lessons.title: Emerson, Thoreau and the Self
lessons.mainIdea: The Transcendentalists argued that truth comes through the individual's own mind and conscience, not through institutions or tradition.
reading: In the 1830s a former minister in Concord, Massachusetts, began giving lectures that made his listeners feel both thrilled and scolded. Ralph Waldo Emerson told them that every person had direct access to truth through intuition and nature. Institutions, he said, were the lengthened shadows of single people, and imitation was suicide. His 1841 essay Self-Reliance is a string of such sentences, each one a small dare. He and his circle were called *Transcendentalists*. They believed the deepest truths transcended, or went beyond, what the senses and logic alone could prove.

Transcendentalism was America's version of *Romanticism*, the European movement that valued feeling, imagination, nature and the individual over reason, rules and society. But the Concord writers gave it a practical edge. If conscience is the highest authority, then a person must act on it. Emerson's most famous student took him at his word. Henry David Thoreau built the cabin at Walden Pond in 1845 to test how simply one could live, and wrote Walden, published in 1854, about the two years he spent there.

Thoreau's night in jail produced Civil Disobedience, and its central claim answers Edwards directly: the conscience that Edwards would terrify into submission, Thoreau treats as the one authority a person must never surrender. His sentences are built for quoting. He writes that under a government which imprisons anyone unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison. A century later Gandhi in India and Martin Luther King Jr. in the American South read the essay and used it.

The Transcendentalists could be naive; they trusted the self more than the self may deserve. But their argument set the terms for much of what followed. Whitman's celebration of himself, Dickinson's private universe, even Huck Finn's decision to follow his heart against his teaching, all work out what Emerson and Thoreau started. In America, they argue, the individual conscience is where the real authority lives.

words.d: Emerson, Thoreau and their circle, who believed truth comes through the individual's intuition and conscience
a movement valuing feeling, imagination, nature and the individual over reason and social rules
Emerson's ideal of trusting one's own mind rather than tradition or the crowd
a person's inner sense of right and wrong

look.title: The Just Man's Place
look.text: Under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison.
look.cite: Henry David Thoreau, Civil Disobedience (Resistance to Civil Government), 1849
look.prompt: Thoreau spent one night in jail and someone else paid his tax. Does that weaken the sentence, or does the sentence stand on its own as an argument?

check.q: Why were Emerson and his circle called Transcendentalists?
choices: They believed the deepest truths go beyond what senses and logic alone can prove
They lived above a store in Concord
They rejected all belief in truth
They wanted to transcend the United States and return to England
check.why: They held that intuition and conscience reach truths that reason cannot prove.

check.q: How does Thoreau's Civil Disobedience answer Edwards, according to the lesson?
choices: It agrees that fear leads to grace
It treats the conscience as the one authority a person must never surrender
It argues that the government is always right
It rejects religion entirely
check.why: Where Edwards terrifies the conscience into submission, Thoreau makes it the highest authority.

check.q: Which later writers does the lesson say worked out the Transcendentalist idea of the individual conscience?
choices: Bradstreet and Edwards
Paine and Jefferson
Whitman, Dickinson and Twain's Huck Finn
Swift and Frost
check.why: Whitman's self, Dickinson's private universe and Huck's decision all extend Emerson and Thoreau's claim.

lessons.title: The Dark Side of Romanticism
lessons.mainIdea: Hawthorne, Poe and Melville shared the Romantics' interest in the inner life but saw guilt, madness and obsession where Emerson saw light.
reading: Not every American Romantic believed in the sunny self. Nathaniel Hawthorne lived in Concord for a time and knew Emerson, but his fiction is full of secret sin and public shame. His 1850 novel The Scarlet Letter follows Hester Prynne, forced by a Puritan town to wear a red letter A for adultery. The father of her child, a respected minister, hides his guilt until it destroys him. Hawthorne's own ancestor had been a judge in the Salem witch trials. He used the Puritan past to ask what a community does to the people it condemns.

Edgar Allan Poe, who died in 1849, went inward and down. His narrators bury enemies alive, watch themselves go mad, and cannot escape their own minds. Poe also invented the modern detective story and wrote about how a story should produce a single effect in the reader, planned from the first sentence. Where Emerson trusted the individual mind, Poe made it the most frightening place in the world.

Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, from 1851, sets a Transcendentalist temptation on a whaling ship. Captain Ahab has lost a leg to a white whale and hunts it across the oceans as if it were evil itself. His crew follows a single will to destruction. The narrator, Ishmael, survives to tell it. The novel takes Emerson's confident self and asks what happens when that self is wounded, obsessed and in command of other people.

Critics sometimes call these three writers *Dark Romantics*. They are not anti-Romantic; they share the movement's fascination with the individual, with nature and with the imagination. But they answer Emerson's optimism with a question: what if the self, looked at honestly, contains things that cannot be trusted? Guilt in Hawthorne, madness in Poe, obsession in Melville. The argument between these two sides of Romanticism is one of the great conversations in American writing.

words.d: Hawthorne, Poe and Melville, who explored guilt, madness and obsession within the Romantic interest in the self
a fixed idea that takes over a person's mind, like Ahab's hunt for the whale
Poe's principle that every detail of a story should build one planned emotional result
to judge someone guilty and unworthy, as Hester's town judged her

look.title: Two Views of One Mind
look.text: Emerson tells a young reader: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. Poe's narrator in The Tell-Tale Heart also trusts himself completely, and his trust leads him to murder and then to confession. Melville's Ahab trusts his own will and takes a ship down with it.
look.prompt: Is Poe's narrator a refutation of Emerson's advice, or a warning about misreading it? What would Emerson say self-trust requires that Ahab lacks?

check.q: What question does Hawthorne use the Puritan past to ask in The Scarlet Letter?
choices: Whether Puritans should have crossed the Atlantic
What a community does to the people it condemns
Whether poetry should rhyme
How whaling ships were built
check.why: Hester's public shaming and the minister's hidden guilt show the town's judgment at work.

check.q: What does the lesson say Moby-Dick asks about the Transcendentalist self?
choices: Whether it can be taught in schools
Whether it belongs in poetry
What happens when that self is wounded, obsessed and in command of others
Whether it needs a church
check.why: Ahab is the confident self turned to obsession, and his crew follows him to destruction.

check.q: Why are Hawthorne, Poe and Melville called Dark Romantics rather than anti-Romantics?
choices: They wrote only at night
They rejected the individual and the imagination
They lived far from Concord
They share the Romantic interest in the self but find guilt, madness and obsession inside it
check.why: They answer Emerson's optimism with a question, not with a rejection of his subject.

lessons.title: Whitman and Dickinson
lessons.mainIdea: Whitman and Dickinson invented two opposite poetic voices, one vast and public, one compressed and private, and both broke the rules of verse.
reading: In 1855 a printer and journalist from Brooklyn published a thin book of poems with no author's name on the cover. There was only a picture of a bearded man in work clothes with his hat tilted. The book was Leaves of Grass, and the man was Walt Whitman. Its long poem, later titled Song of Myself, opens by celebrating the speaker's own self. It declares that every atom belonging to him belongs equally to the reader. Whitman wrote in *free verse*, lines without regular meter or rhyme, each as long as a breath. He cataloged everything in America he could see: carpenters, prostitutes, presidents, the runaway slave he shelters in one section.

About the same time, in Amherst, Massachusetts, Emily Dickinson was writing poems no one would read for decades. She wrote nearly eighteen hundred; fewer than a dozen were published in her lifetime, and those against her wishes or altered by editors. Her poems are short, packed, and strange, full of dashes, unexpected capital letters, and *slant rhyme*, where sounds nearly match but not quite. She wrote about death, God, pain and the mind in the meter of hymns, and then broke the hymn from inside.

Set the two side by side. Whitman's line spills across the page and includes everyone; Dickinson's line stops short and admits almost no one. Whitman writes I am large, I contain multitudes; Dickinson writes I'm Nobody. Yet both are doing what Emerson asked: trusting the self absolutely and making a new form to fit it. Both were also reworking the earlier American voices, Whitman answering Paine's public prose with public poetry, Dickinson answering Bradstreet and Edwards with a private faith that questions everything.

Nearly all later American poetry descends from one of them. Poets who want to include the whole country in a long line look back to Whitman. Poets who want to say the most in the fewest words look back to Dickinson. Learn to hear both, and you will hear the two poles of the American voice.

words.d: poetry without regular meter or rhyme, shaped by breath and phrase
a rhyme in which the sounds nearly match but not exactly, as in 'soul' and 'all'
a long list in a poem, one of Whitman's favorite devices
the regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of verse

look.title: The Hymn Inside a Dickinson Stanza
rows: Because I could not stop for Death,
The carriage held but just ourselves
look.cite: counted for this lesson; Emily Dickinson, first stanza of the poem beginning 'Because I could not stop for Death,' published 1890
look.prompt: The 8-6-8-6 pattern is the meter of many church hymns. What is the effect of using a hymn's rhythm for a poem in which Death is a polite gentleman caller?

check.q: What is free verse?
choices: Poetry that is given away
Poetry without regular meter or rhyme
Poetry written only in the first person
Poetry with exactly eight syllables per line
check.why: Whitman's lines follow breath and phrase rather than a fixed meter or rhyme scheme.

check.q: How many of Dickinson's poems were published in her lifetime, approximately?
choices: About eighteen hundred
About half of them
Fewer than a dozen
None at all
check.why: She wrote nearly eighteen hundred poems; fewer than a dozen appeared in print while she lived.

check.q: What do Whitman and Dickinson have in common, according to the lesson?
choices: Both wrote long lines that catalog America
Both trusted the self absolutely and made new forms to fit it
Both published widely and were famous in their lifetimes
Both used the meter of hymns
check.why: Their voices are opposite in size and reach, but both answer Emerson's call to trust the self and invent a form.

lessons.title: Frederick Douglass Learns to Read
lessons.mainIdea: Douglass's Narrative uses the story of his own literacy to argue that slavery depends on keeping minds in the dark.
reading: Frederick Douglass was born enslaved in Maryland around 1818. He escaped to the North in 1838, and in 1845 he published Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, Written by Himself. Those last three words were an argument. Many white readers doubted that a formerly enslaved man could write such a book. Douglass put his own name on the title page and named the people who had held him, at real risk of being captured and returned.

A *slave narrative* is a first-person account of life in slavery and escape from it, and hundreds were published before the Civil War. Douglass's is the most famous because it is a work of literature as well as testimony. Its center is the story of reading. His mistress in Baltimore began teaching him letters until her husband stopped her, saying that learning would make a slave unmanageable. Douglass writes that this speech was his first clear lesson: the pathway from slavery to freedom ran through the alphabet. He then taught himself, trading bread to poor white boys for lessons.

The Narrative is built as an argument as much as a memoir. Each incident is chosen to prove a point. Slavery corrupts the enslavers. Religion was used to justify cruelty. An enslaved person's mind was fully human and fully capable. The book's most famous sentence turns the story on its hinge. The reader has seen how a man was made a slave, and will now see how a slave was made a man. Douglass fights back against a brutal overseer named Covey. From that day, he says, he was free in spirit whatever his legal status.

Douglass is answering everyone before him. Against Edwards, he shows religion used for evil and demands a better one. Against Paine and Jefferson, he asks how a nation founded on liberty could hold him. Alongside Emerson and Thoreau, he shows self-reliance not as a lecture topic but as a fight in a farmyard. In 1893 he spoke at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, an old man still arguing with his country.

words.d: a first-person account of life in slavery and escape from it, published to argue against slavery
the ability to read and write
a first-hand account offered as evidence of what happened
a man hired to supervise and punish enslaved workers on a farm

look.title: The Hinge of the Narrative
look.text: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
look.cite: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845
look.prompt: The two halves of the sentence mirror each other with the words reversed. What does the structure of the sentence itself argue about slavery and freedom?

check.q: Why does the lesson call the words 'Written by Himself' an argument?
choices: They proved the book was short
Many white readers doubted a formerly enslaved man could write such a book
They were required by law on all books
They showed Douglass had a publisher
check.why: The phrase asserted the author's full humanity and ability against a doubting audience.

check.q: What lesson did Douglass draw from his master's speech forbidding his reading lessons?
choices: That reading was dangerous to his health
That his mistress had been wrong to teach him
That the pathway from slavery to freedom ran through literacy
That he should stop trying to learn
check.why: The master's fear told Douglass exactly what slavery depended on: keeping minds in the dark.

check.q: How does Douglass answer Emerson and Thoreau, according to the lesson?
choices: He shows self-reliance as a physical fight for freedom, not a lecture topic
He rejects self-reliance as selfish
He argues that nature is more important than conscience
He refuses to write in the first person
check.why: His fight with Covey is self-reliance lived, in a farmyard rather than a lecture hall.

lessons.title: Harriet Jacobs and the Hidden Years
lessons.mainIdea: Jacobs's narrative tells what Douglass's could not: how slavery bore down on women, and how she hid seven years in a tiny attic to free her children.
reading: Harriet Jacobs was born enslaved in Edenton, North Carolina, in 1813. Her 1861 book, Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, was published under the name Linda Brent, with the names of people and places changed. Its subject was too dangerous to print openly: the sexual pursuit of enslaved women by the men who owned them. Jacobs addressed her book directly to the free women of the North. She asked them to imagine her situation before judging her choices.

The book's most astonishing section describes her hiding place. To escape her owner and to be near her two children, Jacobs hid in a crawlspace under the roof of her grandmother's house. The space was about nine feet long and seven wide, with a sloping roof so low she could not stand. She stayed there for nearly seven years. She watched her children through a small hole she bored in the wall, unable to speak to them. She wrote later that her body suffered badly. Still, she would rather live in that loophole than in the comfort of slavery.

Douglass's story moves outward and upward: from ignorance to reading, from a farmyard fight to escape to a lecture platform. Jacobs's moves inward and stays: into a garret, for years, for her children. The two narratives together show that slavery was not one experience. Douglass writes of manhood won; Jacobs writes of motherhood defended. Reading both, you see what each account leaves out and what the other supplies.

For many years scholars doubted that Jacobs had written her own book, assuming a white editor had. Research in the 1980s, using her letters, established that the book was hers. That history is itself part of the American argument: whose voices get believed, and what proof is demanded of them. Jacobs, like Douglass, wrote her way into the record, and the record eventually caught up.

words.d: a small attic space under a roof; Jacobs hid in one for nearly seven years
a false name used by an author, such as Linda Brent
to speak or write directly to a particular audience
in Jacobs's book, a small hole and by extension her hiding place; also a narrow way out

look.title: Nine Feet by Seven
look.text: Picture a space about the size of a large closet, with a roof that slopes so low you cannot stand. No window; a hole the width of a finger to see through. Summer heat, winter cold, insects, silence. Outside the wall, your children playing, who do not know you are there. Now picture staying for seven years.
look.prompt: Jacobs said she would rather live in that loophole than in the comfort of slavery. What does her choice tell you about the word comfort as it was used to defend slavery?

check.q: Why did Jacobs publish under the name Linda Brent?
choices: Her real name was hard to spell
Her subject was dangerous to print openly and she protected real people and places
Women were not allowed to publish books in 1861
Her editor chose the name for sales
check.why: The book's subject, sexual pursuit of enslaved women, required changed names for safety.

check.q: How does the lesson contrast the movement of Douglass's story and Jacobs's?
choices: Douglass's moves outward and upward; Jacobs's moves inward and stays for her children
Douglass's is fiction; Jacobs's is fact
Douglass's is about the North; Jacobs's about the West
Douglass's has no argument; Jacobs's does
check.why: His narrative climbs toward escape and the platform; hers descends into a garret and endures.

check.q: What did research in the 1980s establish about Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl?
choices: That it was written by Douglass
That it was a novel
That Jacobs was its true author
That it was first published in 1811
check.why: Her letters proved the book was hers, ending long doubt about its authorship.

lessons.title: Twain and the Realist Turn
lessons.mainIdea: Realism after the Civil War aimed to show ordinary life and ordinary speech truthfully, and Twain made a boy's dialect carry a moral argument.
reading: After the Civil War, American writers turned away from the Romantic interest in the ideal and the strange, toward ordinary people in ordinary places, speaking the way they actually spoke. This turn is called *Realism*. Mark Twain, born Samuel Clemens in Missouri in 1835, spent his youth on the Mississippi River as a printer, a riverboat pilot and a journalist. He had an ear for American speech that no writer before him had shown on the page.

Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, published in the United States in 1885, is narrated by an unschooled boy in his own *dialect*, the regional speech of the Missouri river country. That choice was itself a Realist statement: the voice of the book belongs to the least respectable person in it. Huck floats down the river with Jim, an enslaved man escaping to freedom, and the book's moral center is the moment Huck decides not to turn Jim in. He has been taught that helping Jim is a sin. He tears up the letter that would betray him and says, all right, then, I'll go to hell.

The sentence is the whole argument of the book. Huck's conscience, shaped by a slaveholding society, tells him one thing; his feeling for Jim tells him another, and he chooses the feeling and accepts damnation. Twain is answering Edwards, whose sermon threatened exactly that hell. He answers Emerson by showing that conscience itself can be corrupted by teaching. He answers Douglass by putting a white boy through the discovery that a Black man is a man.

The novel is not simple. Its final chapters, in which Jim is treated as a plaything in a boy's game, have troubled readers for more than a century, and its use of a racial slur hundreds of times makes it painful to read aloud. Those problems are part of studying it honestly. Realism promised the truth about American life, and the truth included the ugliness that Twain both exposed and, at times, fell into.

words.d: a movement after the Civil War aiming to show ordinary life and speech truthfully
the speech of a particular region or group, with its own words, sounds and grammar
everyday spoken language, as opposed to formal or literary language
the moment or idea in a text where its deepest values are decided

look.title: Huck's Decision
look.text: All right, then, I'll go to hell
look.cite: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, chapter 31, 1885 (United States edition)
look.prompt: Huck believes he is choosing sin. The reader knows he is choosing good. Which kind of irony is that, and what does it accuse?

Ideal heroes on great quests

lessons.title: Naturalism: Crane, London, Chopin, Wharton
lessons.mainIdea: Naturalist writers showed people shaped and often crushed by forces they cannot control: nature, society, heredity and chance.
reading: In January 1897 Stephen Crane was aboard a ship carrying guns to Cuba when it sank off Florida. He spent thirty hours in a ten-foot dinghy with three other men before reaching shore. His story The Open Boat, published that year, begins with the men unable to see the sky because they are watching the waves. The sea in the story is not evil and not kind; it simply does not care whether they live. That indifference is the heart of *Naturalism*, a movement that grew out of Realism and pushed it toward the forces beyond human control.

Naturalist writers treated people almost as scientists treat specimens, shaped by heredity, environment and chance. Jack London's To Build a Fire, in its 1908 version, follows a man in the Yukon who ignores an old-timer's warning. He tries to travel alone at seventy-five degrees below zero. His fingers freeze, his fire fails, and the cold kills him without malice. His dog trots off toward the camp where there is food and warmth. Crane had done something similar in The Red Badge of Courage in 1895. He showed a soldier's courage and cowardice as reactions no nobler than instinct.

Society was a force too. Kate Chopin's The Story of an Hour, from 1894, gives a wife one hour of believing her husband is dead, an hour in which she whispers to herself that she is free. Then he walks in unharmed and she dies, and the doctors call it joy. Chopin's 1899 novel The Awakening, about a woman who refuses the roles of wife and mother, was condemned so widely that her career never recovered. Edith Wharton's The House of Mirth, from 1905, watches New York society destroy a woman who cannot afford to belong to it and will not sell herself to stay.

Naturalism answers the Transcendentalists most sharply of all. Emerson said trust yourself and nature; Crane's sea and London's cold do not care about the self, and Chopin's and Wharton's societies punish it. Yet the best Naturalist stories are not simply bleak. The men in the open boat feel a brotherhood they never felt on land. Chopin's wife has her hour. What these writers deny is the guarantee that the self will win. What they keep is the dignity of the attempt.

words.d: a movement showing people shaped by forces beyond their control: nature, society, heredity and chance
lack of concern; the Naturalist sense that the universe does not care about human beings
traits passed from parents to children; one of the forces Naturalists studied
the physical and social surroundings that shape a person

Nature is a kind teacher
Every individual can succeed through will

check.why: Crane's indifferent sea and London's cold show nature that does not care whether people live.

That the cold was not really dangerous
That the man reached the camp too

choices: Because Naturalists lived in Concord

check.why: Emerson's trust in self and nature meets a sea that does not care and a society that punishes.

lessons.title: Dunbar and the Voices to Come
lessons.mainIdea: Paul Laurence Dunbar became the first widely famous Black American poet, and his poem about the mask points toward the Harlem Renaissance.
reading: Paul Laurence Dunbar was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1872, the son of parents who had been enslaved in Kentucky. He was the only Black student in his high school class and edited the school paper. After graduation the only work he could find was running an elevator. In 1893 he traveled to Chicago for the World's Columbian Exposition, where he met Frederick Douglass. Douglass hired him as a clerk and praised him publicly. By 1896 Dunbar was famous across the country, the first Black American poet to reach a wide national audience.

Dunbar wrote in two voices. Many of his most popular poems used a Black Southern *dialect* that white readers found charming and that Dunbar came to feel trapped by. His poems in standard English were often more bitter and more direct. The most famous, We Wear the Mask, from 1895, describes a mask that grins and lies, hiding cheeks and eyes, worn over torn and bleeding hearts. The poem never names race. It does not have to. Every Black reader in 1895 knew what mask it meant, and the poem's restraint is its force.

Dunbar died of tuberculosis in 1906 at thirty-three. Fifteen years later a young poet named Langston Hughes published his first major poem, The Negro Speaks of Rivers, in 1921. Hughes belongs to the *Harlem Renaissance*, the flowering of Black art, music and writing in the 1920s, which is beyond this chapter's range and you will study elsewhere. But its writers read Dunbar, argued with his dialect poems, and carried his mask forward. Dunbar is the hinge between Douglass's generation and theirs.

Here the chapter's long argument comes round. Bradstreet kept her voice inside a rigid faith. Douglass and Jacobs wrote their way into a record that doubted them. Dunbar wrote of a mask that the country made him wear. Each is asking what America is and whether it includes them. The Harlem Renaissance would answer with a whole movement. For now, the thing to hear is how the question got there: passed from writer to writer, each one refusing the last one's silence.

words.d: the flowering of Black American art, music and writing centered in Harlem in the 1920s
the speech of a particular region or group; Dunbar wrote many poems in a Southern Black dialect
holding back; saying less than could be said, for greater force
the point where one thing turns into another; Dunbar as the link between two generations

look.title: The Mask
look.text: We wear the mask that grins and lies, / It hides our cheeks and shades our eyes,— / This debt we pay to human guile; / With torn and bleeding hearts we smile,

look.prompt: The poem says 'we' and never says who 'we' are. What does the poem gain by leaving that unsaid, and who is the 'we' asking the reader to become?

They were too hard to write

check.why: The poem's power comes from saying less than it could and trusting the reader to know.

Paine's first pamphlet

Dialect narration

choices: Defended the king
Argued in plain, spoken-style prose for full independence
Used only Latin quotations
Was written in verse

choices: the majority is always right
taxes should be higher
one should never break any law

review.q: How do Hawthorne, Poe and Melville differ from Emerson?
choices: They rejected the individual as a subject
They wrote only about Europe
They found guilt, madness and obsession where he found light
They refused to use imagery
review.why: The Dark Romantics share Emerson's interest in the self but distrust what they find inside it.

review.q: What is the most important contrast between Whitman and Dickinson?
choices: Whitman rhymed and Dickinson did not
Whitman's line is vast and public; Dickinson's is compressed and private
Whitman lived in Amherst and Dickinson in Brooklyn
Only Whitman broke the rules of verse
review.why: Both broke the rules, but in opposite directions: the long catalog and the packed short line.

choices: It tells the experience of enslaved women, which his could not
It is shorter
It was published first
It is set in the North
review.why: Jacobs writes of sexual pursuit and motherhood defended; Douglass writes of manhood won.

choices: Nature is a friendly teacher of the self
